court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: In an action for conversion of a piano, the Appellate Term held that a boarding-house keeper's statutory lien extends only to accrued charges for board and lodging actually furnished, not to future rent or damages for breach of an alleged yearly room hiring at a weekly rate, and ordered a new trial to determine when the tenant's surrender of the room was accepted.

notes: Room was rented from a boarding-house keeper on a weekly rate under an alleged yearly hiring; treated by the court under ordinary landlord-tenant surrender doctrine, limiting the boarding-house lien to lodging actually furnished.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: The Appellate Division held that restrictive covenants prohibiting noxious, noisy, or objectionable business and limiting occupancy to two families are not violated by a private family taking boarders into its own dwelling, even where the boarders are occasionally noisy, since such conduct is not a 'business' within the meaning of the covenants.

quotes.text: Restrictive covenants in a deed prohibiting dangerous, noxious, noisy and objectionable business, and restricting dwelling houses to the use of two families, are not violated where an owner takes boarders, and this is so, even though it be shown that the boarders congregate about the premises, play games and are noisy.

Upon what theory the taking’of boarders in and by a private family, in their dwelling house, can be deemed to be a violation of the restrictions specified, as the trial court evidently has decided, I do not understand.

In practically every suburb of New York city, such as Hount Vernon, New Rochelle or White Plains, in which nearly all of the newer sections have quite as stringent restrictions as these, the taking of boarders in private houses in such sections has been carried on for years, without any question of its violating such a restriction having been even raised.
